title: Basics of winpipes
text: winpipe connections can set wait requests responses. Similar base connections, winpipe() supports blocking argument. set TRUE, connection blocks R session side pipe responds. exemplify, going set background R session using callr. client connects, server keep waiting blocking. non-blocking client connects, return immediately return nothing server time respond. blocking client connects, wait server responded thus return server’s greeting.
code: start_server <- function() {   callr::r_bg(function() {     message("Waiting for client...")     srv <- winpipe::winpipe(       "winpipe-block",       open = "w",       server = TRUE,       blocking = TRUE     )     message("A client connected!")     Sys.sleep(3)     writeLines("hello", srv)     close(srv)   }) } srv <- start_server() while (!np_exists("winpipe-block")) Sys.sleep(0.1) cat(srv$read_error()) #> Waiting for client... cli <- winpipe(   "winpipe-block",   open = "r",   server = FALSE,   blocking = FALSE )  system.time(x <- readLines(cli)) #>    user  system elapsed  #>       0       0       0  x #> character(0)  close(cli) srv$kill() #> [1] TRUE srv <- start_server() while (!np_exists("winpipe-block")) Sys.sleep(0.1)  cli <- winpipe(   "winpipe-block",   open = "r",   server = FALSE,   blocking = TRUE )  system.time(x <- readLines(cli, n = 1)) #>    user  system elapsed  #>    0.00    0.00    2.97  x #> [1] "hello"  close(cli) srv$kill() #> [1] FALSE

title: Basics of winpipes
text: Even non-blocking request/response behavior can controlled using peeking. Peeking allows us retrieve size payload reading check message delivered big . reading , payload consumed. opens two mechanisms. First, lets implement custom blocking reads callbacks. example, server waits minimum payload size 50 bytes sent. allows client stagger request. Second, opens possibilities handle payloads based size. example, server accepts payloads less 20 bytes. client sends larger one, declines closes pipe instance.
code: srv <- winpipe("example-peek", server = TRUE) cli <- winpipe("example-peek", server = FALSE)  writeLines("here is a payload", cli) np_peek(srv) #> [1] 18  readLines(srv) #> [1] "here is a payload" np_peek(srv) #> [1] 0 while (np_peek(srv) < 50) {   writeLines("and another one", cli)   message("payload not big enough")   Sys.sleep(0.5) } #> payload not big enough #> payload not big enough #> payload not big enough #> payload not big enough readLines(srv) #> [1] "and another one" "and another one" "and another one" "and another one" writeLines("here is a really really really big payload") #> here is a really really really big payload if (np_peek(srv) > 20) {   writeLines("payload is too big", srv)   close(srv) }  readLines(cli) #> character(0)  close(cli)

title: fifo() vs. processx vs. winpipe
text: Named pipes live \\.\pipe\ namespace. Every pipe machine listed list.files("//./pipe/"), ones ship Windows access controlled, make poor examples. Instead, create helper function ps_server() starts tiny server using PowerShell. Open details see works. ps_server() starts server background. mode decides client connects: send line UTF-8 ("out8") UTF-16 ("out16"), read line (""), echo line back ("echo").
code: ps_script <- tempfile(fileext = ".ps1") writeLines(' param($name, $mode, $msg, $log) $dir = if ($mode -eq "out8" -or $mode -eq "out16") { "Out" }        elseif ($mode -eq "in") { "In" } else { "InOut" } $s = New-Object System.IO.Pipes.NamedPipeServerStream($name, [System.IO.Pipes.PipeDirection]::$dir) $s.WaitForConnection() if ($mode -eq "out8") {   $w = New-Object System.IO.StreamWriter($s)   $w.WriteLine($msg); $w.Flush() } elseif ($mode -eq "out16") {   $enc = New-Object System.Text.UnicodeEncoding($false, $false)   $w = New-Object System.IO.StreamWriter($s, $enc)   $w.WriteLine($msg); $w.Flush() } elseif ($mode -eq "echo") {   $r = New-Object System.IO.StreamReader($s)   $w = New-Object System.IO.StreamWriter($s)   $line = $r.ReadLine()   # The client may already be gone, e.g., if it failed to write   try { $w.WriteLine("echo: $line"); $w.Flush() } catch {} } else {   $r = New-Object System.IO.StreamReader($s)   $r.ReadLine() | Out-File -Encoding ascii $log } Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 1000 $s.Dispose() ', ps_script)  ps_server <- function(name, mode, msg = "", log = "") {   system2(     "powershell",     c("-NoProfile", "-ExecutionPolicy", "Bypass", "-File", shQuote(ps_script),       name, mode, shQuote(msg), shQuote(log)),     wait = FALSE   )    for (i in 1:100) {     if (name %in% list.files("//./pipe/")) return(invisible())     Sys.sleep(0.1)   }   stop("Pipe '", name, "' was not created") }

title: fifo() vs. processx vs. winpipe
text: Unix, fifo() opens FIFO create mkfifo. Windows, R implements Win32 named pipes, different semantics: Opening reading ("r") connects existing pipe client. Opening writing ("w") creates pipe, .e., R becomes server. connect pipe already exists. Data read written UTF-16, bytes. last point easy miss. peer sends ordinary UTF-8 ASCII text, readLines() returns nothing: connection opened without error, server saw client, bytes decoded wide characters discarded. peer happens send UTF-16, text arrives: "w" creates pipe, fifo() also write existing server. Opening "r+" mode connects, writing fails: fifo() can used two R processes expect UTF-16, talk arbitrary program. request/response protocol HTTP possible.
code: ps_server("demo-fifo-utf8", "out8", "hello from powershell")  con <- fifo("\\\\.\\pipe\\demo-fifo-utf8", "r", blocking = FALSE) for (i in 1:10) {   res <- readLines(con)   if (length(res)) break   Sys.sleep(0.2) } res #> character(0) close(con) ps_server("demo-fifo-utf16", "out16", "hello from powershell")  con <- fifo("\\\\.\\pipe\\demo-fifo-utf16", "r", blocking = FALSE) for (i in 1:10) {   res <- readLines(con)   if (length(res)) break   Sys.sleep(0.2) } res #> [1] "hello from powershell" close(con) ps_server("demo-fifo-echo", "echo")  con <- fifo("\\\\.\\pipe\\demo-fifo-echo", "r+", blocking = FALSE) try(writeLines("hello", con)) #> Error in writeLines("hello", con) : cannot write to this connection close(con)

text: winpipe exposes Win32 named pipe native R connection. client connects server = FALSE, can read write pipe, every R function accepts connection works. echo server demonstrates request/response exchange: winpipe also reads UTF-8 external servers, like processx: Opening client "r" "w" requests access, can also connect one-way pipes processx reader: winpipe can also server, accept clients without blocking R session, take security descriptor. title: Low-level information about a named pipe — np_config
text: Functions retrieve low-level information named pipe. np_config() returns pipe configuration. np_state() returns current clients. np_peek() looks bytes pipe without reading. np_connected() checks client server connected side pipe. np_sd() returns security descriptor.

title: Low-level information about a named pipe — np_config
text: con [winpipe]. open winpipe created winpipe. warn [logical(1)] Whether warn pipe peeked . np_peek() run without error even pipe can technically read connected anything. case, signals warning returns 0. Set TRUE reading disconnected pipe intended.

title: Low-level information about a named pipe — np_config
text: np_config() returns: is_server is_client: Whether pipe started server client. is_message_type is_byte_type: Whether pipe reads data bytes messages. Pipes created using winpipe always read bytes. out_buffer_size in_buffer_size: Size input output chunks. max_instances: Maximum allowed instances. np_state() returns: state: reading mode pipe. Can either blocking non-blocking byte-mode message-mode. Pipes created using winpipe always blocking byte-mode. current_instances: Number instances related pipe. username: con server, reports username current client, . con client, NA. np_peek() returns number bytes available read pipe. np_peek() read pipe, returns error code warning. np_connected() returns TRUE con server client connected con client server connected. side connected, returns FALSE. np_sd() returns object class winpipe_sd.

(error 109) #> [1] 0  close(cli)

title: Security token information — np_whoami
text: Query Windows access token associated named pipe client calling R process. np_whoami() returns information token's user. np_token_info() returns full token details.

title: Security token information — np_whoami
code: np_whoami(con = NULL)  np_token_info(con = NULL)

title: Security token information — np_whoami
text: con [winpipe] NULL. server end connected pipe, query connected client's token, NULL (default) query token R process .

title: Security token information — np_whoami
text: np_whoami() returns string form "DOMAIN\\user". np_token_info() returns list : user: possible, user name "DOMAIN\\user". sid: user SID string. groups: data frame group names, SIDs, whether group enabled. elevated: whether token elevated, .e. runs admin rights. integrity: integrity level, .e., objects can client touch? Can one : "low": low-permission users, e.g., protected apps sandboxes "medium": standard users "high": admin users "system": OS services token_type: "primary" (process) "impersonation" (pipe client). impersonation_level: level server can impersonate. Can one : "anonymous": server obtain information "identification": server can identify client's SID groups "impersonation": server can act client locally "delegation": server can act client locally remotely NA: primary tokens

title: Security token information — np_whoami

code: # np_proxy() is a good way to communicate with named pipes # that communicate over HTTP, e.g., docker if (np_exists("docker_engine") && requireNamespace("httr2")) { library(httr2)  proxy <- np_proxy("docker_engine") on.exit(proxy$proc$kill())  # GET requests, e.g., to query the docker version resp <- request(proxy$base_url) %>%   req_url_path("/version") %>%   req_perform() %>%   resp_body_json() resp[c("Version", "ApiVersion", "Os")]  # POST requests, e.g., to create a container # do not run this if you don't wish to modify your docker state if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # pull image pull <- request(proxy$base_url) %>%   req_url_path("/images/create") %>%   req_url_query(fromImage = "hello-world", tag = "latest") %>%   req_method("POST") %>%   req_perform() pull$status_code  # create container created <- request(proxy$base_url) %>%   req_url_path("/containers/create") %>%   req_url_query(name = "winpipe-test") %>%   req_body_json(list(Image = "hello-world:latest")) %>%   req_perform() created$status_code } # } }
